title: Best Eyeshadow Palettes 2026: Naked vs Anastasia Soft Glam
description: Five eyeshadow palettes compared on pigmentation, blendability, fallout, warm vs cool tones, and price — from budget ColourPop to luxury Natasha Denona.
lede: A palette can look stunning in the pan and apply like chalk on your lid. The difference between a palette you reach for daily and one that gathers dust is pigmentation, blendability, and fallout — three things the swatch on the website never tells you honestly.

sections.heading: Top pick: Urban Decay Naked Palette
paragraphs: The Urban Decay Naked palette is the best all-round eyeshadow palette because it set the standard for versatile, everyday neutrals that genuinely perform. The Naked range pairs a balanced mix of matte and shimmer shades — wearable browns, taupes, and warm or neutral tones with a few smoky deepening shades — that take you from a soft daytime wash to a full evening smoky eye with one palette. Crucially, the formula is the benchmark: richly pigmented so colours show up true on the lid, buttery and easy to blend without going muddy, and low on fallout for shimmers.

Its enduring appeal is that it's the palette that flatters almost everyone and teaches you how to do eye makeup. The neutral-leaning shade range suits all skin tones and eye colours, the matte transition shades make blending forgiving for beginners, and the shimmers are the kind that apply smoothly with a fingertip or a brush. Urban Decay's quality control means the shades are consistent and the shimmers don't crumble — the hallmarks of a palette worth its price.

The honest caveats: it's a premium drugstore-to-mid price (more than ColourPop, less than luxury), and because it's neutral-focused it's not the palette for someone craving bold colour. But for the single most versatile, reliably high-performing, flatters-everyone palette that does daytime and night, the Urban Decay Naked is the default — the one to own if you own one.

sections.heading: Best for a defined glam look: Anastasia Soft Glam
paragraphs: The Anastasia Beverly Hills Soft Glam palette is the pick for someone who wants polished, defined, glamorous eye looks — the warm-neutral 'soft glam' aesthetic that dominates wedding, event, and night-out makeup. It's a thoughtfully curated mix of mattes and shimmers in warm browns, soft pinks, a touch of mauve, and gorgeous metallic shades, designed so the whole palette works together to build a sculpted, dimensional eye with a luminous lid.

Anastasia is renowned for matte formulas specifically — the mattes here are richly pigmented, velvety, and blend like a dream, which is the hard part of any palette, since chalky or patchy mattes ruin a look. The shimmers are intense and foil-like when applied wet. It's a favourite of makeup artists for client work precisely because it reliably delivers that camera-ready, defined-but-soft glam finish, and the shade range flatters a wide variety of skin tones with its warm bias.

The trade-offs: it's a premium-priced palette, it leans warm (so cool-toned-makeup lovers may want something else), and the curated glam focus means it's more 'going out' than 'quick everyday.' But for anyone who loves a defined, luminous, sculpted eye and wants the mattes-and-shimmers that make glam looks easy, the Soft Glam is the standout — and it's the palette many people buy as their 'special occasion' workhorse.

sections.heading: The bold pick, the luxury option, and the budget champion: Huda, Natasha Denona, ColourPop
paragraphs: The Huda Beauty Rose Gold palette is the pick for intense colour and dramatic, statement looks. Huda is famous for some of the most pigmented, foiled, show-stopping shimmers in the business — the metallic and duochrome shades apply like liquid foil and genuinely turn heads — alongside rich mattes that bring drama. The Rose Gold palette in particular is beloved for its warm rose, copper, and burgundy tones that flatter and pop. It's the choice for someone who wants colour payoff and glamour rather than subtle neutrals, and who enjoys a bolder, more editorial eye.

The Natasha Denona Mini palette is the luxury pick, offering the brand's legendary formula in a more accessible, smaller format. Natasha Denona is widely regarded as making some of the best eyeshadow formulas in the world — almost impossibly smooth, intensely pigmented, and effortlessly blendable, with shimmers that are unmatched for their multidimensional, reflective finish. The mini palettes give you that ultra-premium formula in a curated, travel-friendly size at a price far below the full palettes, making the brand's quality finally attainable. It's for the enthusiast who wants the very best formula and will appreciate the difference.

The ColourPop Going Coconuts (and similar) palette is the budget champion that punches absurdly above its price. ColourPop offers genuinely good pigmentation, fun curated shade stories, and creamy, blendable formulas — both mattes and their signature pressed-glitter and metallic shades — at a price so low you can own several. The quality isn't flawless (some shades are stronger than others and the very cheapest shimmers can have fallout), but the value is extraordinary, making it perfect for beginners experimenting, anyone who wants to try bold colours without commitment, or building a varied collection cheaply.

sections.heading: How to choose: pigmentation, blendability, finish, and tone
paragraphs: Judge pigmentation and blendability first, because they determine whether a palette is usable. Pigmentation is how true and strong the colour shows up on your lid versus in the pan — weak, sheer shadows that need ten layers are frustrating, while well-pigmented ones (Urban Decay, Anastasia, Huda, Natasha Denona) deliver colour in one or two passes. Blendability is how smoothly shades melt into each other without going patchy or muddy — the hardest thing to get right, especially for mattes, and where premium brands like Anastasia and Natasha Denona pull ahead. A beautifully pigmented but unblendable palette is a chore; prioritise formulas reviewers consistently call 'buttery' and 'blendable.'

Match the finish mix and tone to the looks you want. Most palettes balance matte shades (for transition, definition, and a soft everyday look) with shimmer/metallic shades (for a luminous, glam lid) — a good everyday palette needs enough mattes, especially mid-tone transition shades, to make blending easy, while glam and bold palettes lean harder on intense shimmers. Also check the warm-versus-cool bias: warm palettes (browns, golds, oranges, the Anastasia and Huda here) flatter many skin tones and suit cosy, glam looks, while cool palettes (taupes, greys, mauves) suit different looks and skin undertones. Pick the tone family you'll actually wear.

Buy for your skill level and how much you'll use it. Beginners are best served by a versatile neutral palette with plenty of forgiving matte transition shades (Urban Decay Naked) or an inexpensive one to practise with (ColourPop) — bold, highly-pigmented colour palettes are less forgiving of mistakes. Enthusiasts who've mastered blending will appreciate paying up for the very best formulas (Natasha Denona) or specialised glam and colour palettes (Anastasia, Huda). And be realistic about fallout (shimmer flecks dropping onto your cheeks during application) — it's common with intense glitter shades; tapping off excess and doing eyes before face makeup manages it, but consistently low-fallout formulas are worth seeking out if it bothers you.

faqs.q: What makes an eyeshadow palette good — what should I look for?
faqs.a: Three things matter most: pigmentation, blendability, and fallout. Pigmentation is how strongly and truly the colour shows up on your lid compared to how it looks in the pan — good palettes deliver rich colour in one or two passes, while poorly pigmented ones need endless layering and still look sheer. Blendability is how smoothly the shades melt together without becoming patchy or muddy, which is the hardest quality to achieve (especially in matte shades) and where premium brands like Anastasia and Natasha Denona excel. Fallout is the shimmer flecks that drop onto your cheeks during application — lower is better, and it's most common with intense glitter shades. Beyond those, consider the shade range and finish mix (enough matte transition shades for easy blending, plus shimmers for glam), and the warm-versus-cool tone. A palette that's well-pigmented, blends beautifully, and has manageable fallout is one you'll actually reach for, regardless of how pretty it looks in the pan.

faqs.q: Are expensive eyeshadow palettes actually better than cheap ones?
faqs.a: Sometimes meaningfully, sometimes not — it depends where you are on the skill and usage spectrum. The biggest differences premium palettes (like Natasha Denona, Anastasia, Urban Decay) deliver are formula quality: smoother, more pigmented, more effortlessly blendable shadows with less fallout and better, more reflective shimmers, plus consistency across all the shades in the palette. For enthusiasts who blend a lot and notice the difference, that's genuinely worth paying for. But budget brands have closed the gap enormously — ColourPop, for instance, offers genuinely good pigmentation and creamy formulas at a fraction of the price, with the trade-off being some shade-to-shade inconsistency and occasionally more fallout. For a beginner, a practising teen, or anyone who wants to experiment with colours without commitment, an inexpensive palette is the smart choice and you won't be missing much. The sweet spot for most people is a quality mid-range neutral palette like the Urban Decay Naked that you'll use constantly, supplemented by cheap fun palettes for variety.

faqs.q: How do I stop eyeshadow fallout from ruining my face makeup?
faqs.a: Fallout — the shimmer or pigment flecks that drop onto your cheeks during eyeshadow application — is common, especially with intense glitter and metallic shades, but it's manageable. The single most effective trick is to do your eye makeup before your face makeup (foundation and concealer): that way, any fallout lands on bare skin and you simply wipe it away, then apply your base over a clean canvas. Beyond that, tap excess product off your brush before applying (a generous tap against the palette edge), pat shimmer shades onto the lid rather than sweeping them, and use a fluffier brush with a lighter hand for loose-pigment shades. Some people also hold a tissue or a 'shadow shield' under the eye to catch fallout. Choosing palettes with lower-fallout formulas helps too — pressed shimmers and well-bound metallics (as in better-quality palettes) drop far less than loose glitter shades. None of these fully eliminate it with the most intense shimmers, but doing eyes first is the fix that always works.
